neutral_facts.value: The accused, along with others, were part of an unlawful assembly with the common object of eliminating the deceased by criminal force. The deceased was assaulted by the other accused persons with weapons such as kanta and knives, resulting in his death. The accused in question fired a shot from a country-made pistol into the air to frighten the witnesses and then fled the scene. The post-mortem report confirmed multiple injuries on the deceased, indicating the assault was homicidal. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence to establish the involvement of the accused in the unlawful assembly and the murder.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the appellant was part of an unlawful assembly and that the eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2 stated that the appellant was carrying a country-made pistol and fired in the air to frighten the informant and others, thereby enabling the accused to escape. The prosecution also emphasized the motive rooted in property disputes and old enmity between the families.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's involvement in the actual murder, as there were no firearm injuries, no recovery of a country-made pistol or cartridges, and the scribe Kuldeep Kumar Tiwari and Laxmi Narain, who could have provided crucial evidence, were not examined as witnesses. The defence also claimed the conviction was based on mere suspicion.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle under Section 149 IPC, which holds that every member of an unlawful assembly is vicariously liable for the offence committed in prosecution of the common object, even if they did not directly participate in the act.
